challenges.title: Rotate an Array
challenges.prompt:
Given an array `nums` and a non-negative integer `k`, rotate the array to the right by `k` steps: each item moves `k` places toward the end, and items that fall off the end wrap around to the front.

Modify `nums` in place using O(1) extra space, then return `nums` so the tests can check it.

examples.explain: The last three items wrap around to the front.
Rotating by 3 is the same as rotating by 3 % 2 = 1.

hints: Rotating by n leaves the array unchanged, so only k % n matters.
Reversing the whole array puts the last k items at the front, but backward.
Reverse everything, then reverse the first k items, then reverse the remaining n - k items.

solution.python:
def rotate(nums, k):
    n = len(nums)
    k %= n

    def reverse(lo, hi):
        while lo < hi:
            nums[lo], nums[hi] = nums[hi], nums[lo]
            lo += 1
            hi -= 1

    reverse(0, n - 1)
    reverse(0, k - 1)
    reverse(k, n - 1)
    return nums

challenges.explanation: Reduce k with k % n. Reversing the whole array moves the last k items to the front in reverse order; reversing the first k items and the last n - k items separately restores the order inside each block. Every item is swapped a constant number of times.

challenges.title: Product of Array Except Self
challenges.prompt:
Given an integer array `nums`, return an array `answer` where `answer[i]` is the product of every item in `nums` except `nums[i]`.

Solve it in O(n) time without using division. Every product fits in a 32-bit integer.

examples.explain: Only the position of the zero skips the zero.

hints: The product of everything except nums[i] is (the product of the items to its left) times (the product of the items to its right).
Fill the answer array with left products in one pass from the start.
Walk back from the end with one running right product and multiply it into each answer.
challenges.explanation: The first pass stores in answer[i] the product of everything left of i. The second pass walks from the right with a running product of everything right of i and multiplies it in. No division is needed, so zeros are handled naturally.

complexity.space: O(1) extra besides the output array

challenges.title: Longest Common Prefix
challenges.prompt: Given a list of strings `words`, return the longest string that every word starts with. If the words share no common prefix, return an empty string.

examples.explain: All three start with "fl", but the third letters differ.

hints: Compare the words one column (character position) at a time, using the first word as the reference.
Stop at the first column where some word has a different character or has already ended.
Check the word's length before you read the character, so you never index past the end of a short word.
challenges.explanation: Scan column by column against the first word. The prefix ends at the first column where any word disagrees or runs out of characters. If no column fails, the whole first word is the prefix.

complexity.time: O(S), where S is the total number of characters

challenges.title: String Compression
challenges.prompt:
Compress a string by replacing each run of the same character with the character followed by the length of the run, so `"aabcccccaaa"` becomes `"a2b1c5a3"`.

If the compressed string is not strictly shorter than the original, return the original string instead. Letters are case-sensitive.

examples.explain: "a1b1c1" is longer, so return the original.

hints: Find each run with two indexes: i marks its start and j moves forward while the character matches.
Collect the pieces in a list and join once at the end; repeated += can be quadratic.
Compare lengths at the end and return the original on a tie.

solution.python:
def compress(s):
    parts = []
    i = 0
    while i < len(s):
        j = i
        while j < len(s) and s[j] == s[i]:
            j += 1
        parts.append(s[i])
        parts.append(str(j - i))
        i = j
    out = "".join(parts)
    return out if len(out) < len(s) else s

challenges.explanation: Walk the string run by run: j advances past every copy of s[i], so j - i is the run length. Each character is visited once, and the parts are joined once at the end. Multi-digit counts such as 12 work because str() writes the whole number.

challenges.title: Palindrome After One Deletion
challenges.prompt: Given a string `s`, return `true` if it is already a palindrome or can become one by deleting at most one character. Otherwise return `false`.

examples.explain: No single deletion makes it read the same both ways.

hints: Walk two indexes inward from both ends while the characters match.
At the first mismatch, one of those two characters must go, and you cannot tell which. Try both.
Each try is a plain palindrome check on the remaining range, so the total work stays O(n).
challenges.explanation: Match characters from both ends. Everything outside the first mismatch already pairs up, so the only question is which of the two mismatched characters to delete. Check the range without the left one and the range without the right one; if either is a palindrome, the answer is true. Trying only one side fails on inputs like "abbab".

challenges.title: Balance Point Index
challenges.prompt:
Given an integer array `nums`, return the leftmost index where the sum of all items strictly to its left equals the sum of all items strictly to its right. Missing items count as 0, so index 0 has a left sum of 0 and the last index has a right sum of 0.

If no such index exists, return `-1`.

examples.explain: 1 + 7 + 3 = 11 on the left and 5 + 6 = 11 on the right.
The left sum is 0 and the right sum is 1 + (-1) = 0.

hints: Recomputing both sides from scratch for every index is O(n^2).
If you know the total and the running sum of everything to the left, the right sum follows by subtraction.
right = total - left - nums[i]. Check the condition before adding nums[i] to left.
challenges.explanation: Compute the total once. Walking left to right, keep the sum of the items already passed; the right sum is whatever remains after removing the left sum and the current item. The first index where they match is the answer.
